item.description:

A threat actor dubbed Gheist is turning compromised GitHub accounts into credential-harvesting platforms. By planting malicious GitHub Actions workflows in private repositories, the attackers can expose repository and environment secrets, then retrieve them through GitHub APIs before deleting evidence of the activity.

Tracked since September 15 by Wiz Research, the campaign has left more than 13,500 malicious branches across over 850 compromised accounts, spanning personal projects and private enterprise repositories.

The campaign’s weapon is GitHub Actions, the platform’s automation service, which attackers are using to turn stolen access into harvested credentials. The automation creates a branch, adds a workflow named “sync-check” that attempts to print secrets into execution logs, retrieves those logs through the GitHub API, and deletes the workflow run seconds later.

item.title: 🟠 Your AI agent learned a better way. Who approved the change?
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Imagine a support team working through complaints after a service outage. Its refund policy normally requires an eligibility review. For this incident, an authorized manager approves an exception: customers on the verified outage list may receive up to $100 without individual review, through Friday.

An agent processes those cases successfully. Later, the system consolidates those case histories into a reusable memory: small, immediate refunds resolve service complaints quickly. The summary preserves the outcome but loses the outage restriction and expiration date.

The following week, the agent retrieves that guidance for a similar complaint from a customer who was not affected by the outage. It issues a refund without review. The payment service checks the agent’s credentials and the dollar limit, but does not check whether the customer qualifies for an active exception.

No attacker is needed in this hypothetical. The case may close faster, yet the agent has begun applying a temporary exception beyond its authorized scope.

Take for example, Fertitta Entertainment, with more than 600 Landry’s restaurants and the Golden Nugget hotel and casino. After the pandemic, the company had problems adequately staffing its call centers, says its director of contact center operations Brian Jeppesen. “The agents didn’t want to come back,” he says.

The virtual assistants didn’t work because the user experience was bad, and with the incoming call volume, 40 to 50% of them were abandoned.

The moment arrives after the damage. An agent has cancelled a supplier contract, approved a refund it should have declined or moved a customer record somewhere it should never have gone. Someone senior asks a simple question. Why did it do that? The engineering team opens the logs. There are thousands of lines. Every call is timestamped. Every tool invocation is recorded. And nobody in the room can say why the agent chose what it chose.

This pattern is becoming familiar. It will become more so. Logging in most enterprises is mature. Security teams have spent two decades building collection pipelines, retention policies and search tooling. The natural assumption is that this investment transfers to AI agents. It does not. Instead of relying on malware, cybercriminals are increasingly abusing AI tools enterprises depend on — a trend some experts describe as “living off the AI land.” The expanded abuse of AI ecosystems features a growing array of tactics, including poisoned models, compromised MCP servers, prompt injection attacks, and AI supply-chain vulnerabilities.

AI and hybrid work have written new rules for matching a device to a role. Equipping the workforce by persona was once a straightforward exercise: the org chart supplied the groups, a stereotype supplied the requirements, and the model held because most people worked roughly the same way. That no longer holds. AI keeps redrawing what roles need, and hybrid work has scattered where they need it. Together, those two shifts have changed the inputs persona building runs on.

The inputs changed, and the principle held. Smart device fleets still get provisioned by sorting employees into representative types and equipping each accordingly. item.description:

A vulnerability in Google’s Brotli compression library could allow attackers to execute arbitrary code in applications that use an affected Brotli decoder to process compressed data.

Tracked as CVE-2026-111497, the high-severity flaw was first flagged in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js. The issue stems from an out-of-bounds write that can corrupt process memory, potentially leading to remote code execution (RCE), information disclosure, or denial of service (DoS).

The Node.js project disclosed the vulnerability on October 21, 2026, alongside security updates for its 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x release lines. The exposure, however, extended beyond Node.js, forcing Microsoft to release out-of-band security updates for.NET on October 25 to address the same CVE in its Brotli decompression implementation.

item.title: 🔵 ‘Citizen AI’ can help IT leaders spark business solutions — if done right
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

AI fluency has long mattered to Sambit Dutta. When he joined global chemical manufacturer Hexion this year as SVP of AI transformation, his strategy included bringing “AI to the masses, where the people can not only just consume AI, but also become what we call builders.”

Dutta has made citizen AI a cornerstone of Hexion’s IT strategy because he believes that when the creativity and domain expertise of employees is centralized and funneled through a business analyst or developer, “there are always things lost in translation.” Further, “there’s a queuing process where that request ultimately gets queued, and then based on dollars and other priorities, never gets executed,” he adds.

Dutta also believes that innovation unleashed at the grassroots level is how enterprises achieve true transformation. And it facilitates change management because people become more receptive to absorbing technology at that level, he says.

“We firmly believe that we are at a stage where citizen development has finally taken off” at Hexion, Dutton says.

item.description:

Two leading AI developers have released fresh evidence of a problem that researchers have long anticipated: advanced models searching for ways around the limits imposed on them. New disclosures from OpenAI and Anthropic detail how frontier systems exploited weaknesses in their environments or exceeded the intended scope of assigned tasks.

item.title: 🔵 Malicious downloads can trick AI coding agents into compromising themselves
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Malicious instruction files planted in a computer’s Downloads folder can trick AI coding agents into executing harmful code or exposing authentication tokens, Forever Security said after blocking an attempted attack on a customer’s machine and demonstrating similar techniques against OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code.

In its research report, the firm said it discovered a malicious AGENTS.md file in a customer’s Downloads folder that instructed Codex to install a malicious npm package called function-color. The installation was blocked before the malware could execute.

The researchers could not determine how the original file reached the computer, but demonstrated that a malicious website could trigger a similar download without a separate approval prompt.

item.title: 🔵 CIOs rethink roles, skills, training, and talent models for the future
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

Longtime IT leader Matt Ausman envisions a future where developers may not have any backlog because AI will let them create new capabilities as quickly as they imagine them.

“The backlog will vanish because you will have infinite capacity,” says Ausman, SVP and CIO of Zebra Technologies.

He wonders whether business users will be able to keep up with the training required in a world where the software they use will change that rapidly. He also wonders whether IT workers are ready for that scenario: Will they be able to push back on bad ideas, or just build new capabilities simply because they can do so as rapidly as they’re proposed?

“Today we have to prioritize because we don’t have unlimited capacity. But in the future will they stop to ask, ‘Are we building the right things?’” he says, adding that “because someone thought it up, doesn’t mean it’s worth doing.”

item.title: 🟠 The metric that makes your IT org look healthier than it is
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

An executive IT dashboard can stay green for a year while the risks it is supposed to surface keep growing. Availability above target every month. Service levels met. Patch compliance climbing quarter over quarter. Every number accurate, and every one trusted by the executive team.

When trouble finally arrives, it skips amber entirely. It comes as an outage, an audit finding or a security incident, and the first question in the room is why the dashboard said everything was fine.

In my work with technology leaders and executive teams, I have learned that a dashboard can be technically accurate and still leave leadership dangerously misinformed. Usually nobody fudged anything. The numbers were built to summarize, and a summary is very good at hiding the one thing an executive most needs to see. Three metrics produce most of that false comfort at the executive level. I would not put any of them in front of a CEO or a board as a headline number.

item.title: 🔴 What EvilTokens teaches us about defending against AI-assisted attacks
item.description:
Why this matters: Elevated ransomware risk — validate backups, endpoint protection, and recovery readiness.

Cybercriminals don’t need AI to compromise an organization, but AI is making its way into classic attack methods and changing how quickly such attacks can progress. Tasks that once required attackers to manually sift through information and piece together how an organization operates can be accelerated by AI, reducing the time defenders have to detect and intervene.

A recent example of this is EvilTokens, a phishing-as-a-service platform that helps attackers gain access to Microsoft 365 inboxes and then uses AI to analyze the environment to determine the most effective next steps. First identified in February 2026, EvilTokens exploits the device authorization grant flow of OAuth 2.0 to gain access to Microsoft accounts without having to create fraudulent login pages. After taking down Storm-2992, the threat actor believed to be behind the scheme, in September, Microsoft said the EvilTokens operation leveraged AI “at every step of the attack chain.”

item.title: 🟠 Your senior engineers need junior questions more than juniors need answers
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

When juniors take naive questions to an AI assistant instead of a colleague, dashboards record fewer interruptions and higher velocity. What they miss is the erosion of senior engineers’ architectural fluency, and the single point of failure that hardens until an outage forces someone to explain the system out loud.

Over the past year, I watched engineering teams celebrate a quiet drop in Slack interruptions. A junior used to ask a foundational question in a channel: why does this service retry three times instead of once? Today that junior asks an AI assistant first, messaging a senior only if the answer fails in testing. Already, 51% of developers ask generative AI for help they once asked a colleague, and 62% do so to avoid looking uninformed.

item.title: 🟠 Bright Security Introduces STAR Fuzzer, Agentic Fuzzing That Writes Its Own Harnesses and Proves Every Finding
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

Built on an evolutionary engine first released in 2018, STAR Fuzzer by Bright Security finds crashes, memory exhaustion and memory-safety bugs in security-critical code without a running application. In its first open source research run, it found High or Critical issues in 45% of the projects tested, and in its first month of availability it produced ten published findings in eight projects, including the Crystal standard library, htop and RIOT OS.

Bright Security, the Agentic Offensive Application Security company, today announced the official launch of STAR Fuzzer, an agentic application fuzzer that automatically identifies security-critical functions, generates a fuzzing harness for each one, searches for faults with an evolutionary algorithm, and delivers every confirmed finding with a byte-exact payload that reproduces it. STAR Fuzzer is a self-contained mode of the Bright STAR platform and is available now at brightsec.com/fuzzer.

item.title: 🟠 Dual BIOS: The laptop security feature SMBs don’t know they need
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Every security checklist starts with the basics: strong passwords, multifactor authentication, spotting phishing, and keeping software up to date. All four protect what happens after a laptop starts. But some attackers are more focused on what happens before.

That’s the domain of the BIOS, the first code that runs when a laptop powers on. It checks the hardware, then hands control to the operating system. Malware planted at this level can load before the operating system does, so it can evade antivirus tools and even survive a drive wipe or reinstall. 

For small and midsize businesses (SMBs), the cost of an incident goes beyond the bill to fix it.  It’s also about the work that stops in the meantime. The Verizon Business 2026 Breach Impact Study (which analyzes cyber insurance claims), found that SMBs suffered losses accounting for up to 7% of their total revenue. It also identified business interruption as the fastest growing source of loss.

item.description:

A judge in New Mexico has fined Meta $25 billion for its flouting of data privacy laws between 2010 and 2021, including its controversial passing of data to Cambridge Analytica.

The action serves as a stark reminder to enterprises not to play fast and loose with data protection legislation, as the consequences could be highly damaging.

Meta faced the court action after it was revealed that data company Cambridge Analytica had improperly obtained personal data that Facebook was holding.

It could have been even worse for Meta. Under New Mexico law, the damages could have been as high as $219 billion, which would have exceeded its revenue for 2025.

Indian digital trust company eMudhra has announced that it is exiting the global SSL/TLS certificate business and is offering customers certificates issued by Sectigo as an alternative, following the compromise of private keys behind eight of its intermediate certificate authorities.

The company’s board decided “to voluntarily withdraw from the global SSL/TLS certificate business,” eMudhra said in a press note. It added that data sovereignty and compliance requirements had increased the business’s complexity and cost.
